The Middle East is also an important trading partner, accounting for about one-third of Uganda’s exports—mainly gold, exports of which have recently doubled due to higher international prices and increased re-export volumes, largely destined for the UAE—and 15 percent of Uganda’s total imports. A prolonged conflict could therefore affect export earnings, trade flows, and logistics costs in addition to its direct effects on energy markets. These channels are manageable under the current baseline, but their combined effect would intensify materially under a prolonged or deeper conflict scenario.

Poverty continued to decline, supported by growth and low inflation, though structural deprivations remain pervasive. The share of Ugandans living below the USD 3.00-per-day line fell to 51.5 percent in FY25, down from 52.9 percent in FY24. Despite sustained GDP growth, the unem-ployment rate remained broadly unchanged since 2021, at 12.2 percent, with informality accounting for 92 percent of employment, and a large gender gap persisted, with the employment-to-population ratio at 53.1 percent for men compared to 37.4 percent for women. Uganda’s latest Multidimensional Poverty Index reveals that 53.1 percent of Ugandans remain deprived across dimensions of health, education, and living standards, dimensions that consumption-based welfare measures alone do not capture

. Addi-tionally, escalation of conflict in the Middle East— which accounts for almost 26 percent of Ugandan exports—could disrupt global demand and severely impact Uganda’s economic growth. Finally, fiscal risks associated with the 2026 election cycle may lead to increased spending and borrowing, undermining bud-get credibility and eroding investor confidence.

Foreword
The global economic environment remains challenging and uncertain, with almost every country in the world struggling to manage multiple crises in the wake of the devastating COVID-19 pandemic. Uganda’s economy has proven strikingly resilient to recent shocks; economic activity accelerated during 2022, and income levels started to rise as firms reopened and employment began to recover. Nevertheless, the country’s growth trajectory is fragile, and several risks could derail the current expansion. Moreover, poverty remains pervasive, and food insecurity poses a persistent threat to the welfare of vulnerable households

. In contrast to the moderation trend in food and energy prices, core inflation exhibited a modest upward trend, rising by 3.9 percent in FY25 compared to 3.0 percent in the same period last year (Figure 9). This was primarily helped drive poverty reduction. Since agriculture is the primary livelihood for 8 out of 10 poor households and the main sector of employment for 7 out of 10 Ugandans, Uganda’s poverty trajectory is strongly influenced by developments in this sector. As such, the sector’s post-COVID-19 recovery played a critical role in reducing poverty, complemented by broader shifts in employment patterns

Uganda has significant untapped agro-industrialization potential, owing to its abundant natural resources, favorable climate, and exten-sive arable land. Primary agriculture drives Uganda’s economy, contributing 24 percent of GDP, 35 percent of export earnings, and employing 68 percent of the labor force; it has enormous potential to create better jobs by bridging the productivity gaps across agricultural value chains. Most poor households depend on sub-sistence farming, making sector transformation critical for poverty reduction and broad-based prosperity. With 80 percent arable land, favorable climate, and diverse agroecological zones, the country possesses natural advantages that surpass regional peers

passages.text: Uganda (BoU) held the Central Bank Rate at 9.75 per-cent since October 2024, maintaining a tight stance to anchor inflation expectations amid external uncer-tainty. The 7-day interbank rate stood at 11.15 percent, reflecting orderly but tight liquidity conditions. High yields on government securities with the 364-day T-bill at 15.1 percent continued to crowd out private credit, keeping commercial lending rates elevated - with the BoU weighted average rate reported at 18.8 percent - and limiting private investment. (Figure 12). Headline inflation remained well below Uganda’s peers, though energy-driven pressures are building

. Headline year-on-year inflation stood at 3.0 percent in April 2026, below the BoU’s 5 percent target and notably lower than the SSA median of 5.8 percent, reflecting Uganda’s more favorable food price dynamics and exchange rate stability. The key emerging pressure was energy: Energy, Fuel and Utilities (EFU) inflation rose sharply to 6.1 percent year-on-year, from 4.1 percent, with petrol and diesel prices rising by 8.7 and 10.8 percent respectively, directly reflecting CME-driven global fuel price increases. (Box 2) Food crop inflation eased to 0.6 percent, providing a meaningful offset, though its durability depends on continued favorable weather conditions

inside.question: How much did Uganda's economy grow in FY25?

passages.text: Uganda’s economic growth remained above 6 percent in FY25, outpacing regional and global averages. Real gross domestic product (GDP) growth accelerated to 6.3 percent, up from 6.1 percent in FY24. Drivers included a recovery in household consumption, a steep acceleration in government spending, and con-tinued investment growth. Dynamic domestic demand and robust agricultural and tourism performance gen-erated broad-based growth across agriculture, industry, and services. As a result, poverty is projected to have declined in FY25. Advanced indicators of economic activity point to continued broad-based economic dynamism, although lower rainfall could constrain agricultural output in early FY26. Uganda’s external position improved, and foreign exchange reserves rose in FY25

Real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) during 9M-FY25 grew by 6.8 percent, up from 6.1 percent a year earlier, mainly driven by improvement in the commodity-producing sectors. In agriculture, improved food crop production—particularly bananas, maize, and beans—was key to the sector’s performance. In the industrial sector, robust manufacturing growth was led by the pharmaceutical sector, followed by increased value addition in construction. In contrast to commodity-producing sectors, the services sector recorded a broad-based deceleration, with growth easing from 6.8 percent in 9M-FY24 to 5.3 percent in the current fiscal year

Source: Constructed by authors using data from theglobaleconomy.com accessed December 2, 2025.

Economic growth in sub-Saharan Africa continues to weaken. Economic activity in sub-Saharan Africa is estimated to have slowed to 3.6 percent in 2022 from 4.1 percent in 2021.2 However, this is 0.3 percentage point higher than the October 2022 forecast, supported by high commodity prices and buoyant domestic demand. Despite multifaceted challenges, the economies of the East Africa Community showed resilient performances. Ethiopia and Uganda maintained strong growth recovery, with real GDP growth estimated at about 6 percent for FY23 and projected to increase to above 6 percent in FY24. Tanzania’s economy expanded by 4.6 percent in 2022, up from 4.3 percent in 2021, and is projected to increase by 5.1 percent in 2023

1.3 Real economy
Kenya’s economic growth in 2023 experienced a cyclical rebound and accelerated despite the challenging environment. Real GDP expanded by 5.6 percent in 2023, an acceleration from the 4.9 percent from 2022. Two consecutive years of drought had dampened agricultural production which, in addition to the tight global fi nancial conditions, brought down overall growth. The 2023 fi gure brings headline growth above its pre-pandemic average (4.6 percent per year between 2011-2019) and well-above potential GDP growth. Had agricultural value-added grown at its average pre-drought rates since 2011, and not considering the sector’s large multipliers across the economy, real growth would have been closer to 5 percent, not far from its historical trend.
